subject: Chemistry
title: Germanium Proves Mendeleev Right
description: Learn Germanium Proves Mendeleev Right in one minute.

hook.text: In 1886, germanium was discovered in a silver mine. Its properties matched Mendeleev's 1871 predictions almost perfectly.

buildup.text: Mendeleev had called it eka-silicon and predicted its atomic weight, density, and oxide formula.

discovery.text: Clemens Winkler isolated it and found: weight 72.6 (predicted 72), density 5.47 (predicted 5.5).

twist.text: Winkler wanted to name it neptunium, but that name was already taken. He chose germanium for Germany.

climax.text: Germanium later became crucial for transistors—the building blocks of every computer.

punchline.text: Predicted in 1871, found in 1886. Now inside your electronics.

quiz.question: How close were Mendeleev's predictions for germanium?
options: Almost exact—weight and density matched within 1%
He got the weight right but density wrong
His predictions were only vaguely close

details.summary: Clemens Winkler discovered germanium in 1886 in the mineral argyrodite, confirming Mendeleev's 1871 prediction of eka-silicon. Germanium's atomic weight, density, boiling point, and chemical properties all closely matched the values Mendeleev had predicted fifteen years earlier.
details.whyItMatters: Germanium's discovery provided the most comprehensive confirmation of periodic table predictions, as more properties matched than for gallium or scandium. Germanium later became the material used in the first transistor.
takeaways: Germanium matched Mendeleev's eka-silicon predictions across multiple properties
Winkler initially thought he had found a new non-metallic element like antimony
Germanium was used in the first transistor at Bell Labs in 1947

faq.question: How closely did germanium match Mendeleev's eka-silicon predictions?
faq.answer: Mendeleev predicted atomic weight 72, density 5.5, and specific heat 0.073. Actual values: atomic weight 72.6, density 5.32, and specific heat 0.076. He also correctly predicted its oxide formula, chloride boiling point, and chemical behavior. The match across so many properties was extraordinary.

faq.question: How did germanium become important in electronics?
faq.answer: Germanium was the semiconductor used in the first point-contact transistor at Bell Labs in 1947 by Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley. While silicon later replaced germanium in most applications due to its superior oxide properties, germanium remains important in fiber optics, infrared optics.
